book.title: Communicate with Mastery
book.subtitle: Speak With Conviction and Write for Impact
book.edition: 1st edition, January 2020 (hardcover; ebook editions also issued). Foreword by Joel Peterson. Title page reads 'How to Speak with Conviction and Write for Impact'; Wiley's product page omits 'How to'. Wiley lists 240 pages (front matter to p. xix, text and index to p. 211).
book.author_credibility: JD Schramm (EdD) founded the Mastery in Communication Initiative at Stanford Graduate School of Business, where Wiley's author note says he served as lecturer in Organizational Behavior from 2007; he co-founded Stanford's LOWKeynotes talk program and has since taught at NYU Stern and USC Annenberg and coaches executives and speakers. Kara Levy (credited 'with Kara Levy') is an executive communication and leadership coach with a Columbia MFA in fiction who coached at Stanford GSB. Joel Peterson (Stanford GSB lecturer, former JetBlue chair) wrote the foreword and is not a co-author. The book is practitioner and teaching based: Schramm openly borrows several frameworks (AIM from Russell and Munter, the sparkline from Nancy Duarte, the pitch structure from Chris Lipp, Radical Candor from Kim Scott) and draws mostly on classroom and coaching cases rather than original research.
book.evidence_base: Verified from the Wiley Chapter 1 excerpt, the Wiley table of contents and index PDFs, and the GBV scanned contents: the book rests on teaching and coaching anecdotes (named students, clients, Stanford colleagues) and on frameworks from practitioner books (Russell and Munter's Guide to Presentations, Duarte's Resonate and slide:ology, Osterwalder and Pigneur's Business Model Generation, Lipp's The Startup Pitch, Scott's Radical Candor, Heath and Heath's Made to Stick, Knaflic's Storytelling with Data, Abrahams's Speaking Up Without Freaking Out). The index shows it also mentions Amy Cuddy and Dana Carney on power poses (pp. 27-28) and Albert Mehrabian (pp. 29-30), both of which are contested or commonly misapplied findings; I could not read how the book frames them. It has a short bibliography (p. 187) and a recommended bookshelf (Appendix D). It does not present original empirical research.

insights.name: AIM: Audience, Intent, then Message
insights.explanation: Before drafting anything, answer three questions in a fixed order. Audience: who exactly will receive this, what do they already know and care about, and who is the secondary audience (the people your listeners will pass it on to, or who might see it unintentionally). Intent: what you want them to think, say, or do as a result, framed from their side rather than yours ('I want to impress them' is about you). Message: only then choose the channel (from highly to minimally interactive, oral, written, or blended) and the structure. The ordering is the point: most people jump straight to the message. The book opens with AIM because Schramm uses it at the start of nearly every class and coaching session, and he credits the model to Lynn Russell and Mary Munter's Guide to Presentations rather than claiming it.
insights.when_to_use: At the start of any planned communication: a presentation, an email to a senior leader, a proposal, a hard conversation, or even a toast. Especially useful when you feel stuck on what to say, which usually means intent is unclear.
insights.worked_example: A product manager needs budget for a usability study. Her first draft email opens with three paragraphs on research methodology. Running AIM: the audience is a finance director who cares about cost avoidance and has five minutes; the intent is a yes on 18,000 dollars by Friday; so the message becomes a two-line ask up top, the cost of a failed launch last year as the reason, and the methodology moved to an attachment. At home the same week, she uses AIM before talking to her teenager about a curfew: the intent is agreement on a rule he will actually follow, not winning the argument, so she opens by asking what he thinks is fair.
common_mistakes: Defining intent as something about yourself ('impress them', 'inform them') instead of what the audience should think, say, or do
Ignoring the secondary audience, such as the senior partner who will actually decide, or the unintended reader of a forwarded email
Defaulting to a meeting or an email without considering the full range of channels
steps: Write one sentence describing the primary audience and one for the secondary audience: role, prior knowledge, what they care about, how much attention they will give
Research them: online sources, a contact who knows them, and ideally a small test audience
Write the intent as an observable action from the audience's side: 'After this, they will ...'
Choose the channel by asking how far the message must travel, how long it must last, how formal it is, and how interactive it needs to be
Draft the message structure, then check every section against audience and intent and cut what serves neither
situations: Planning a presentation to senior leadership
Writing an email that asks for a decision
Preparing a pitch to investors or a client
Raising a sensitive topic with a family member

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Part 1, Chapter 1 (Adopting a Communication Mindset), section 'Know Your AIM', pp. 3-14
source.underlying_research: The book credits the model to Lynn Russell and Mary Munter, Guide to Presentations (Figure 1.1 source line, p. 4). Audience analysis is long-standing consensus in rhetoric and business communication; the book cites no experimental study for it.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the Chapter 1 excerpt and highlighted by Matt Abrahams on Five Books. Strong practitioner and teaching consensus in business communication curricula, but not an empirically tested framework as such.

insights.name: ABC Writing: Active, Brief, Clear
insights.explanation: The book's core standard for written work is that it should be Active, Brief, and Clear. Active means the person or team doing the action appears first and the real verb is visible (for example 'we decided' rather than 'a decision was made', and 'decide' rather than 'make a determination'). Brief means editing hard: removing filler phrases, repetition, and padding until every sentence earns its place. Clear means the reader can find your main point and requested action quickly, without having to reconstruct your logic. The three checks are designed to be applied as an editing pass after the first draft, not while drafting.
insights.when_to_use: Every piece of writing someone else must act on: emails, status updates, memos, performance reviews, cover letters, even messages to a landlord or school.
insights.worked_example: An operations lead drafts: 'It has been determined that a review of the vendor onboarding process will be undertaken in Q3 due to the fact that there have been a number of delays.' ABC pass: 'We will review vendor onboarding in Q3 because three of the last five vendors started late.' Actor first, real verb, 37 words to 17, and a concrete reason. He later uses the same pass on an email to his child's school, turning a long apology-filled paragraph into a clear request for a meeting time.
common_mistakes: Using passive voice to avoid naming who is responsible, which reads as evasive
Cutting so much that context the reader needs disappears (brief is not the same as cryptic)
Hiding verbs inside nouns such as 'conduct an analysis of' instead of 'analyze'
steps: Draft freely without editing
Active pass: for each sentence, ask who is doing what, and put that actor and verb first; turn nominalizations back into verbs
Brief pass: delete filler ('due to the fact that', 'in order to', 'it should be noted'), duplicate points, and throat-clearing openings
Clear pass: confirm the main point and the requested action can be found in the first lines
Read it once as the recipient would, on a phone, and fix anything that slows you down
situations: Writing a project update email
Editing a report before sending it to leadership
Drafting a complaint or request to a service provider
Writing a self-review

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Part 1, Chapter 3 (Writing for Impact: Active, Brief, and Clear), sections Active (p. 46), Brief (p. 47), Clear (p. 48); also The Power of Editing, pp. 53-55, and Appendix A (Power Verbs)
source.underlying_research: The book draws on practitioner style sources (the index lists the SEC's Plain English Handbook, Nora Ephron, Anne Lamott, and Glenn Kramon of the New York Times, Appendix C). No experimental studies named. The advice aligns with plain-language research and with Joseph Williams' work on nominalizations in Style, which is my identification, not a book citation.

insights.confidence_rationale: The ABC structure is confirmed by the table of contents and the index (active voice pp. 46-47, eliminating weak verbs p. 48, reader attention span pp. 47-48). Well aligned with plain-language consensus. The specific editing passes in the steps are my operationalization.

insights.name: The Scan Test: Main Point on the Surface
insights.explanation: A clear document is one whose argument and request survive a skim. If a busy reader looked only at the subject line, headings, and first sentences, they should still know what you are saying and what you need. The book's 'Clear' guidance includes writing informative headlines and headings, and reader notes report it suggests starting headlines with strong action verbs. 'Scan test' is this project's label for checking that, not the book's term.
insights.when_to_use: Longer emails, memos, proposals, and reports going to people with limited time, especially readers more senior than you or reading on mobile.
insights.worked_example: A nonprofit volunteer coordinator writes a two-page proposal to the board for a new weekend program. Her headings were 'Background', 'Details', 'Budget'. After applying the scan test, they become 'Weekend demand is up 40 percent', 'A pilot with 6 volunteers can cover it', 'We need 2,500 dollars and a vote on June 3'. A board member who reads only those lines knows the case and the ask. She uses the same idea for a family group chat about holiday plans: the first line states the proposed dates and asks for a yes or no by Sunday.
common_mistakes: Writing headings that label a section instead of stating its point
Putting the ask in the last paragraph, where skimmers never reach it
Assuming the reader will read every word because the topic matters to you
steps: Write your main point and your ask as two sentences before drafting
Put them in the subject line or opening lines
Turn each heading into a claim
Make each paragraph's first sentence its conclusion
Test: read only subject, headings, and first sentences; if the message is not clear, revise
situations: Sending a proposal to a busy executive
Writing a board or committee memo
Summarizing a long thread for someone who missed it

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 3, section Clear and headline writing (index: headlines/headings, pp. 48-51, 55, 80); Appendix A (Power Verbs)
source.underlying_research: None named in the book as far as I could verify. Related evidence (my identification): Nielsen Norman Group eye-tracking work on F-shaped scanning of web text, and the bottom line up front convention.

insights.confidence_rationale: Writing headings that carry the point is confirmed by the index and reader notes; the full skim test procedure and the 'scan test' name are not confirmed in the book text. Medium rating rests on strong practitioner consensus.

insights.name: What, So What, Now What
insights.explanation: When you report information, synthesize rather than summarize. The book's 'Synthesis > Summary' section in the writing chapter presents 'What, so what, now what' as a way to deliver messages: the fact or development (what), why it matters to this audience (so what), and the action or decision it calls for (now what). A summary leaves the reader to do the thinking; a synthesis does it for them. Chapter 1 makes the same point when it urges students to synthesize case material into clear insights rather than restate it.
insights.when_to_use: Status updates, escalations, debriefs after meetings, reporting data or research results, and any time someone asks 'what's going on with X'.
insights.worked_example: An analyst is asked in a hallway how the customer survey went. Instead of reciting response rates, she says: 'Satisfaction dropped from 82 to 71 percent, almost all of it from onboarding complaints (what). That is the part of the journey we just changed, so it is probably our fault and fixable (so what). I would like to pull two people for a week to interview churned customers; can I get your OK (now what)?' At home, she uses the same shape when telling her partner the car inspection results: what failed, what it means for the budget, and the two options to decide between.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 'what' and calling it an update
Making the 'so what' about you instead of the listener's priorities
Leaving 'now what' vague, such as 'we should keep an eye on it'
steps: State the key fact or development in one sentence
Explain the implication for this specific listener
Name the action, decision, or next step and who owns it
If you need something, make the request explicit and time-bound
situations: Giving a weekly status update
Answering 'how did it go?' from a manager
Writing a post-meeting recap email
Explaining test results or news to a family member

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 3, section Synthesis > Summary, pp. 48-50 ('What, so what, now what' indexed at p. 49); see also Chapter 1, p. 23
source.underlying_research: The structure predates the book: it traces to Terry Borton's 1970 reflective model, later used by Rolfe, Freshwater and Jasper (2001), and Matt Abrahams teaches it for spontaneous speaking. The index lists Abrahams on p. 49, which suggests the book credits him there, but I could not read the page. No empirical test of it as a communication structure is known to me.

insights.confidence_rationale: Now confirmed in the book via the index and table of contents. A widely used structure in education and management practice, but not experimentally validated as a persuasion tool, so Medium.

insights.name: Parachute In: Skip the Preamble
insights.explanation: Start at the most interesting or consequential moment instead of with introductions, agenda, or background. Schramm calls this parachuting in: drop the audience into the heart of the story, then supply only the context needed, leaving names and logistics for later or for whoever introduces you. He pairs it with a 'Goldilocks' rule for detail: too much loses the audience, too little leaves unintended questions. Reader notes on the speaking chapter add that he advises choosing your first and last words deliberately, since openings and closings shape what people remember.
insights.when_to_use: Openings of talks, pitches, stories, and emails; toasts and eulogies; introducing yourself in a networking or interview setting.
insights.worked_example: A hospital nurse speaking at a fundraising dinner had planned to start with her name, unit, and years of service. Instead she opens: 'At 3 a.m. last March, a seven-year-old asked me if she was going to die.' Her name and role follow in one sentence. She writes out and memorizes her last line so she does not trail off. Later that month she uses the same idea in a best-man speech, opening with the moment the couple met rather than thanking everyone first.
common_mistakes: Spending the first minute on logistics, thanks, and self-introduction when attention is highest
Parachuting in with drama that has nothing to do with the point
Leaving the ending to chance and closing with 'so, yeah, that's it' or 'any questions?'
steps: Identify the single most vivid or consequential moment in your material
Open there in one or two sentences
Add only the context the audience needs to follow
Script and rehearse your final sentence so it lands your intent
situations: Opening a keynote or team talk
Giving a wedding toast
Starting a pitch
Writing the first line of a cold email

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 4, section Storytelling, pp. 69-73 ('Parachute in' p. 70; 'Goldilocks theory' pp. 70-71); first and last words in Chapter 2, Verbal component (per reader notes); Schramm, 'How to Tell Your Story for Impact', Stanford GSB Insights (2011); '5 Steps to Sharper Stories', Communication Matters (Substack)
source.underlying_research: None named. Loosely consistent with serial-position (primacy and recency) effects in memory research (Murdock 1962; Ebbinghaus), although those findings come from word-list recall rather than speeches.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the index and in Schramm's own GSB workshop and newsletter. Expert consensus among speaking coaches; support from memory research is indirect (list-recall studies, not speeches).

insights.name: One Thought, One Person
insights.explanation: When speaking to a group, deliver one complete thought to one person while looking at them, then turn and deliver the next complete thought to someone else. This replaces scanning or staring at slides with a series of small conversations, which steadies your pace, reduces filler between thoughts, and makes each listener feel addressed. Reader notes report the book suggests holding eye contact for roughly four to five seconds, the length of a thought, and pairing it with a grounded stance and arms relaxed at your sides rather than tucked at the elbows. Schramm also encourages stepping toward the audience and using gestures rather than staying frozen in place.
insights.when_to_use: Presentations, meetings where you hold the floor, panel answers, and toasts. Adapts to video by treating the camera lens as the person.
insights.worked_example: A junior engineer presenting a design review tends to read from her slides and race. She practices finishing each sentence while looking at one colleague, pausing, then moving to another. Her pace slows naturally and her 'ums' drop because she breathes between thoughts. At a family reunion, she uses the same approach for a short tribute to her grandmother, landing each memory on a different relative.
common_mistakes: Darting eyes across the room mid-sentence (scanning) instead of finishing the thought
Fixating on one friendly face or only the most senior person
Treating the guidance as a rigid timer rather than one thought per person
steps: Break your content into short complete thoughts
Pick one listener and deliver a full thought to them
Pause briefly as you finish
Turn your body slightly and deliver the next thought to someone in a different part of the room
On video, deliver key thoughts to the camera lens
situations: Presenting to a room of colleagues
Answering a question on a panel
Giving a toast or eulogy
Speaking up in a large meeting

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 2, Visual component (eye contact p. 37, gestures p. 38) and Chapter 4 storytelling ('one person with one thought', p. 71); Schramm, 'How to Tell Your Story for Impact', Stanford GSB Insights (2011)
source.underlying_research: None named in the book as far as I could verify. Eye contact research (for example, Kleinke 1986, Psychological Bulletin) links gaze to attention and perceived credibility, but I found no study supporting a precise duration such as four to five seconds.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the index and reader notes, and in Schramm's own workshop advice. The value of eye contact has research support; specific timings do not.

insights.name: Story Spine: Once Upon a Time to Until Now
insights.explanation: A simple sequence of prompts to turn an anecdote into a story with a point: once upon a time (the normal situation), then one day (the disruption), because of that (the consequences), until now (where things stand and what changed). Schramm stresses that the difference between talking and storytelling is intention: you must know the end point you want the audience to reach before you begin. For organizations, he argues stories should center on what changed for people rather than on how busy the organization has been.
insights.when_to_use: Pitches, fundraising, job interviews (behavioral questions), team kickoffs, explaining a change, and personal stories at gatherings.
insights.worked_example: A job candidate is asked about a time she handled a setback. Using the spine: our support team had a steady three-hour response time (once upon a time); then one day a product bug tripled ticket volume (then one day); because of that, I set up a triage rota and a public status page (because of that); until now, response time is under two hours even at peak, and the rota is standard practice (until now). A parent uses the same frame to explain to a child why the family is moving cities, ending on what will be better.
common_mistakes: Telling events in order with no clear disruption or change
Starting without knowing the ending you want the audience to arrive at
Making the story about your activity rather than the outcome for people affected
steps: Decide the end point: what you want the audience to believe or do afterward
Sketch the normal state in a sentence
Name the specific disruption
Describe the consequences, focusing on people
Close with the present state and its meaning for this audience
situations: Answering a behavioral interview question
Pitching a nonprofit program to donors
Explaining a reorganization to a team
Telling a story at a family dinner

source.citation: Schramm interview, 'How To Series: JD Schramm: How to Tell Your Story', PlayFull Podcast (ImpactFull), show notes. Not found in Communicate with Mastery: the book's storytelling section (Chapter 4, pp. 69-82) is indexed for parachuting in, Goldilocks detail, knowing your why, silence, and Freytag's pyramid via Duarte, with no entry for these prompts.
source.underlying_research: The prompts are a shortened form of Kenn Adams' improv 'Story Spine' (which also includes 'every day', 'until finally', and 'ever since then'); Schramm does not credit it on the show notes page. Narrative transportation research (Green and Brock 2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) supports stories for engagement and attitude change, though not this template.

insights.confidence_rationale: I read the show notes page, which is Schramm's own interview, so the attribution to him holds; but I could not confirm the prompts appear in the book. The template itself is practitioner craft. Retained at Low as per user decision.

insights.name: Disclose With Purpose
insights.explanation: Personal disclosure (an illness, a failure, an identity, a loss) can build connection and credibility, but only when it serves the audience and the point. The book has a full section on disclosing personally that draws on Brene Brown's work on shame and links disclosure to clarity of intent. Schramm's own writing adds practical guidance: know why you are telling it; plan how you begin and end so people leave with your message rather than your emotion; if emotion rises, breathe deeply and pause, and neither hide nor dramatize it. Schramm models this himself, having spoken publicly about surviving a suicide attempt.
insights.when_to_use: Deciding whether to mention a personal struggle in a talk, team meeting, or interview; telling colleagues about a diagnosis or life change; coming out at work; sharing a hard family story.
insights.worked_example: A team lead returning from leave after a cancer diagnosis wonders how much to share. She asks what she wants the team to do with the information (adjust workload expectations, not worry or tiptoe). She tells her two closest peers first to test the wording, then gives the team three sentences: what happened, what it means for her schedule, and how she would like them to treat her. She admits she feels awkward saying it, and closes by moving to the agenda. She later uses a similar process to tell extended family.
common_mistakes: Disclosing to gain sympathy or deflect accountability rather than to serve the listener
Sharing far more detail than the audience can process
Improvising an emotional story live without having planned the beginning and end
steps: Ask why you are sharing and what you want listeners to do or understand
Decide what level of detail serves that intent and what stays private
Script your first and last lines
Rehearse from bullet points rather than a word-for-word manuscript
If emotion rises while speaking, breathe slowly, pause or step back, then continue without apologizing
situations: Telling your team about a health issue
Deciding whether to share a personal story in a talk
Coming out to colleagues
Sharing a difficult family history

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 4, section Disclosing Personally, pp. 82-89 (Brown on shame pp. 82-83; intent and self-disclosure p. 83); Schramm, 'Pressing through tears', Communication Matters (Substack); 'Be authentic: Q&A with JD Schramm', TED Blog
source.underlying_research: The book draws on Brene Brown's Daring Greatly (pp. 82-83). Related research (my identification, not book citations): Altman and Taylor's social penetration theory and Collins and Miller's 1994 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin linking disclosure and liking, with appropriateness as a moderator.

insights.confidence_rationale: Section and its link to intent confirmed via the table of contents and index; the procedural advice comes from Schramm's newsletter, which I read. Removed an earlier claim about testing the story on a small group first, which I could not source. Consistent with self-disclosure research.

insights.name: Pause, Verify, Iterate
insights.explanation: Schramm's practical definition of mastery boils down to three habits. Pause before you send, post, or speak, especially when emotional or rushed. Verify that the receiver understood what you meant, rather than assuming that sent equals received. Iterate: use what you learn to improve the next message. None of this makes communication perfect; it makes it steadily better. The habit is particularly valuable in writing and chat, where tone and intent are easily misread and there is no live feedback.
insights.when_to_use: Before sending emails or chat messages with any emotional charge or high stakes; after giving instructions; when a thread is going in circles.
insights.worked_example: A project coordinator drafts a terse Slack reply to a colleague who missed a deadline. She pauses, rereads it as the colleague would, and softens it into a question about what got in the way. After a call with a contractor, she verifies by sending a three-line recap and asking him to confirm the dates. When the contractor's reply shows a misunderstanding, she adjusts her recap template so it lists dates first next time. She does the same with a family group chat about elder care, checking that each sibling read the schedule the same way.
common_mistakes: Treating a lack of reply as agreement or understanding
Pausing only to polish wording, without checking whether the tone fits the relationship
Never closing the loop, so the same misunderstanding repeats
steps: Before sending or speaking, stop and reread from the recipient's point of view
Ask: is the intent clear, and could the tone be misread?
After sending or speaking, check understanding (a recap, a question, asking them to restate next steps)
Note what was misunderstood and change your approach next time
situations: Replying to a frustrating email
Delegating a task
Coordinating family logistics in a group chat
Confirming agreements after a call

source.citation: Schramm, 'Why Mastery Matters', Communication Matters (Substack, December 2024); related to the Introduction of Communicate with Mastery (subsections Iteration, p. xvii, and Feedback, p. xviii)
source.underlying_research: None named. Related evidence (my identification): Kruger, Epley, Parker and Ng (2005), 'Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 89(6), which found senders overestimate how well recipients detect tone.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed as the author's own three-step formulation in his newsletter (read in full); the book's introduction covers iteration and feedback but I could not confirm this exact triad in the book. The verify step is supported by replicated research on overconfidence in written tone.

insights.name: Mastery, Not Perfection
insights.explanation: Communication is a learnable skill, like golf or cooking, not a fixed talent. Schramm borrows Dan Pink's definition of mastery as getting better and better at something that matters: there is no perfect presentation, pitch, or email, so mastery is an aspiration you approach but never reach, and chasing perfection only adds anxiety. The practical engine is self-reflection: after a talk or important message, review what worked and what to change, often from a recording, and turn that into a small number of goals for the next attempt.
insights.when_to_use: When nervous before high-stakes communication, after a talk that went poorly, when building a development plan, or when telling yourself you are 'just not a good speaker or writer'.
insights.worked_example: After a fumbled quarterly review presentation, a sales manager writes down three things that worked (clear opening, good chart on pipeline, calm Q&A) and two to change (ran six minutes over, read the slides in the middle section). Next quarter he cuts two slides and practices the middle section twice. Separately, before a hard talk with his father about moving into assisted living, he lets go of finding perfect words and aims for an honest, reasonably clear conversation he can return to later.
common_mistakes: Reflecting only on what went wrong, which feeds anxiety without improving skill
Listing too many goals at once, so none stick
Assuming one bad performance proves a lack of talent
steps: After a talk or important message, write down two or three specific things that worked
Write one or two concrete changes for next time
Where possible, review a recording or ask one trusted observer
Pick a single focus for the next attempt and check it afterward
situations: Preparing for a nerve-racking presentation
Debriefing after a talk that went badly
Setting personal development goals
Building confidence after criticism

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Introduction (Individuality, Relevance, Iteration, Feedback, Stakes, pp. xiii-xviii); Think Fast, Talk Smart episode with Matt Abrahams (2020); Ideas on Stage Podcast episode 61 (2024); 'Why Mastery Matters' (Substack)
source.underlying_research: The book draws on Dan Pink's Drive for its definition of mastery (index: Pink p. xiv). Related research (my identification): deliberate practice (Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer 1993, Psychological Review) on feedback-driven improvement, and growth-mindset research (Dweck), whose intervention effects have been small in recent large studies.

insights.confidence_rationale: The mastery framing is confirmed by Schramm in the Abrahams interview, where he calls it the premise of the book, and by reader notes. Feedback-based practice is well supported; the specific reflection routine is practitioner advice.

insights.name: Slides Support the Conversation
insights.explanation: Slides are an aid, not the presentation. Each slide should carry one message, built from images, charts, or a headline rather than paragraphs, so the audience grasps it at a glance and returns attention to you. Design the talk first, then decide which points truly need a visual. Reader notes report a specific tip from the book: do not end on a 'Questions?' slide; instead show a strong chart or image from the talk again, or restate your thesis with contact details, and move into Q&A verbally.
insights.when_to_use: Any slide-based presentation, from team updates to conference talks; also when deciding whether to use slides at all.
insights.worked_example: A finance analyst's budget review deck has 22 slides of dense tables. She rewrites each slide title as the single takeaway ('Travel spend is 30 percent over plan, driven by two teams'), shows one simplified chart per slide, and moves the full tables to an appendix sent afterward. When the projector fails in the meeting, she can still deliver the story from her titles. For her book club presentation, she skips slides and brings one printed photo instead.
common_mistakes: Using slides as a teleprompter and reading them aloud
Packing several messages onto one slide
Ending on a generic 'Questions?' slide that wastes the last visual impression
steps: Outline the talk without slides first
Mark the points where a visual genuinely helps understanding
Write each slide title as a full-sentence takeaway
Remove anything on the slide that does not support that one message
Rehearse so you could deliver the talk if the slides failed
situations: Preparing a quarterly business review deck
Presenting research findings
Pitching with a slide deck
Giving a talk at a conference

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 5, section When Using Slides, pp. 107-110 (Q&A slides pp. 104, 107-110; laser pointers pp. 109-110); Schramm, 'How to Tell Your Story for Impact', Stanford GSB Insights (2011)
source.underlying_research: The book points to Nancy Duarte's slide:ology, Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's Storytelling with Data, and Jerry Weisman (index). Related research (my identification): Richard Mayer's multimedia learning principles (coherence, signaling), well replicated in instructional settings.

insights.confidence_rationale: Section confirmed via the table of contents and index; the Q&A slide tip is from reader notes. Removed an earlier anecdote about an event where visuals failed, which I could not source. Aligned with replicated multimedia learning findings.

insights.name: Compensate for the Thin Channel in Virtual Meetings
insights.explanation: Video and phone meetings strip out much of the nonverbal information people rely on, so you need to replace it deliberately. The book's setting chapter has a short section on virtual meetings (pp. 97-99); its index shows it covers eye contact on video, slides in virtual meetings, time zones, audio calls, and Zoom. The underlying idea is that the same AIM thinking applies, but the channel demands more explicit signals of attention, turn-taking, and understanding. The specific techniques below (camera as the listener's eyes, explicit turn-taking, written recaps) are a reasonable reading of those topics, not confirmed book text.
insights.when_to_use: Leading or presenting in video calls, remote interviews, phone negotiations, and long-distance calls with family.
insights.worked_example: A remote team lead notices her video stand-ups are flat and quiet. She checks the time zones so nobody is joining at midnight, starts each call by naming who will speak in what order, looks at the camera when making key points, and ends by asking each person to confirm one next step in chat. On weekly calls with her parents abroad, she asks direct questions rather than an open 'how is everything', because she cannot read their faces well on a frozen connection.
common_mistakes: Presenting to the screen image instead of the camera
Assuming silence means agreement on a call
Speaking in the same flat tone you might get away with in person
steps: Before the call, check time zones and decide how people will participate (order, chat, reactions)
Look at the camera for key points
Use more vocal variety and shorter segments than in person
Check understanding explicitly by name
Summarize decisions in writing after the call
situations: Running a remote team meeting
Presenting on a video call
Doing a video job interview
Keeping in touch with family by video

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 5, section Virtual Meetings, pp. 97-99 (topics per index: eye contact in video meetings p. 98, slides p. 98, time zones and Zoom pp. 98-99); detailed advice not verified
source.underlying_research: None named. Related research (my identification): Bailenson (2021), 'Nonverbal overload: A theoretical argument for the causes of Zoom fatigue', Technology, Mind, and Behavior 2(1), which post-dates the book.

insights.confidence_rationale: The section and its topics are now confirmed via the index, but I could not read its advice, and it is only about three pages. Specific techniques remain thinly sourced to the book. Retained at Low as per user decision.

insights.name: Lower and Slower for Gravitas
insights.explanation: Your voice is a flexible tool. Reader notes on the book's vocal section report that it advises a strong, clear voice and deliberate variation in speed: faster builds energy, slower adds weight. In a 2025 newsletter Schramm goes further: to signal gravitas, drop into a lower register and slow your cadence, because the shift tells listeners this moment deserves attention. The book also warns against uptalk (rising intonation at the end of statements), which undercuts credibility. The same newsletter suggests titling a talk weeks ahead so ideas can develop.
insights.when_to_use: Delivering key messages, decisions, or bad news; opening a talk; any moment you tend to speed up from nerves.
insights.worked_example: A new manager announcing a reorganization notices she speeds up and her pitch rises when nervous. She marks the two sentences that matter most in her notes and practices delivering them more slowly and at the lower end of her natural range, with a pause after each. When telling her kids about a family decision, she uses the same slower pace so they register it as serious rather than offhand.
common_mistakes: Forcing an unnaturally deep voice, which sounds strained
Slowing down everything, which drains energy; save it for key points
Ending statements with rising intonation that sounds like a question
steps: Identify the one or two sentences that carry your key message
Mark them in your notes
Practice them at a slower pace, in the lower part of your comfortable range
Add a short pause before and after
Record yourself and compare with your normal delivery
situations: Announcing a major decision
Delivering bad news to a team
Opening a presentation
Asserting yourself in a tense meeting

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 2, Vocal component, pp. 31-36, and managing derailers (uptalk pp. 42-43), per index and reader notes; Schramm, 'Stretching Yourself', Communication Matters (Substack)
source.underlying_research: Not named by the author. Related research (my identification): Klofstad, Anderson and Peters (2012), 'Sounds like a winner: voice pitch influences perception of leadership capacity in both men and women', Proceedings of the Royal Society B, found lower-pitched voices preferred for leaders; effects are context dependent and raise gender concerns.

insights.confidence_rationale: Slowing for weight and avoiding uptalk are now tied to the book via the index and reader notes; the lower-register advice is confirmed only in the newsletter. Research on pitch and perceived leadership exists but is mixed and context dependent, and the advice risks penalizing natural voices. Retained at Low as per user decision.

insights.name: Clarity Over Conformity in Identity
insights.explanation: The book's identity chapter argues that who you are (language background, sexual orientation, gender, career stage, military service) shapes how you lead and communicate, and that it can be an asset or a liability you need to acknowledge rather than hide. For leaders speaking in a second (or third) language, the index shows the short section focuses on clarity and on slowing your pace to aid comprehension, citing Kara Levy's piece 'Slow Down Your Speech to Speed Up Comprehension'. The practical upshot: aim improvement effort at being understood (pace, structure, visual support), not at erasing identity markers to fit a narrow norm. Other sections offer a 'lavender diamond' of LGBTQ presence (clarity, competence, confidence, connection) and guidance for women, rookies, and veterans.
insights.when_to_use: When you feel pressure to change how you sound or present to fit in; when coaching people from different backgrounds; when deciding how much of your identity to bring into a talk.
insights.worked_example: An engineer who moved from Brazil worries his accent hurts him in design reviews. Rather than taking accent-reduction lessons, he works on slowing slightly, stating his conclusion first, and putting key numbers on a slide so they are not lost. Colleagues start engaging with his ideas more. He also stops apologizing for his English at the start of meetings, which had been undercutting him more than the accent.
common_mistakes: Apologizing for your accent or background before speaking, which primes the audience to discount you
Assuming every communication problem is an identity problem rather than a clarity problem
Coaching others to conform rather than to be clear
steps: Ask whether listeners are actually missing your meaning, and where
Fix those clarity points (pace, structure, visual support for numbers and names)
Drop pre-emptive apologies about how you speak
Decide deliberately which parts of your identity to bring into a message and why
situations: Presenting in a second language
Being the only person of your background in the room
Coaching a colleague who worries about their accent

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 6 (Tailoring Your Communication to Your Identity), pp. 111-137; section Leading in Your Second (or Third, or Fourth) Language, pp. 112-113; Schramm on identity in the Think Fast, Talk Smart interview (2020)
source.underlying_research: The book cites Kara Levy's 'Slow Down Your Speech to Speed Up Comprehension' (p. 113). Related research (my identification): Lev-Ari and Keysar (2010), 'Why don't we believe non-native speakers? The influence of accent on credibility', Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 46(6), shows accent can reduce credibility; later replications have been mixed.

insights.confidence_rationale: Clarity and pace as the focus for second-language speakers are now supported by the index, and the asset-or-liability framing by Schramm's interview. The earlier claim, from a Blinkist summary, that the book says the accent itself is not the issue could not be confirmed. The section is about two pages and evidence is thin. Retained at Low as per user decision.

insights.name: Get Coached, Then Rehearse Together
insights.explanation: The book closes with scaling leadership through coaching, across three chapters: being coached (setting goals, choosing a coach, adopting a coaching mindset), coaching others (what makes a good coach, the coach's role, tools such as video feedback and simple exercises), and building a coaching culture (with Kim Scott's Radical Candor: care personally while challenging directly). Reader notes report that the book advises coaches not to rewrite the speaker's work but to ask guiding questions so the speaker builds the skill. Schramm's own practice adds group rehearsal: coach each speaker individually, then hold a joint dress rehearsal where people learn by watching peers get feedback.
insights.when_to_use: Preparing a high-stakes talk, helping a team prepare for a big pitch or offsite, developing direct reports' communication, or practicing a difficult personal conversation with a friend.
insights.worked_example: A department head has three team members presenting to the executive committee. She meets each one for 30 minutes on content, then runs a group run-through a week before where each presents and gets two strengths and one or two changes in front of the others. People adopt fixes they saw given to peers. A friend uses the same approach before a hard conversation with her ex about custody: she rehearses with a trusted friend, who tells her what landed and one thing to soften.
common_mistakes: Rehearsing only in your head or only alone
Giving or asking for vague feedback ('it was good')
Holding the final rehearsal too late to make changes
steps: Clarify AIM with the speaker before giving delivery feedback
Coach individually on content first
Schedule a group dress rehearsal several days before the event
Give each person specific strengths and one or two specific changes
Ask speakers to self-assess before you give feedback
situations: Preparing a team for a client pitch
Coaching a direct report before a big presentation
Rehearsing a difficult conversation with a friend
Choosing a speaking coach

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Part 3 (Scaling Your Leadership: The Communication Coaching Process), Chapters 7-9, pp. 139-163 (Radical Candor pp. 159-161; video feedback pp. 151-152); Schramm, 'Coaching Cohorts', Communication Matters (Substack)
source.underlying_research: The book draws on Kim Scott's Radical Candor. Related research (my identification): deliberate practice (Ericsson et al. 1993) and Bandura's observational learning.

insights.confidence_rationale: Coaching chapters confirmed via the table of contents and index; group rehearsal practice confirmed in Schramm's newsletter (read). Consistent with feedback and observational learning research.

insights.name: Leadership Communication Canvas
insights.explanation: For high-stakes messages, Schramm expands AIM into a nine-box canvas adapted from Osterwalder and Pigneur's Business Model Canvas. Starting on the right with Audience (primary and secondary), you work through: Value Proposition (why you are the right messenger), Channels, Connections (what will engage the audience, such as a story or question), Assets and Resources (stories, data, images you have or need), Activities (how you get the right people to show up or read), Partners (designers, champions, critics who can help), Message Structure, and Results (what you want them to think, say, or do). The boxes can be tackled in any order. For structure he recommends Nancy Duarte's sparkline: move back and forth between what is and what could be, ending on a call to action. He uses the canvas only when the stakes are high, not for every email.
insights.when_to_use: Major announcements, keynotes, campaigns, fundraising pitches, change initiatives, or any message that must reach several audiences through several channels.
insights.worked_example: A school principal must win support for a later start time. Audience: parents, but also teachers and the bus contractor as secondary audiences. Value proposition: she has the attendance data, but a pediatrician on the parent council is more credible on sleep, so she invites him as a partner. Channels: a short email, a town hall, and a one-page FAQ. Assets: a chart of first-period tardiness and one student's story. Activities: asking the parent association to promote the town hall. Structure: she alternates between today's tired mornings and what a later start could look like, ending with a request to complete a survey by Friday. Results: 60 percent survey support.
common_mistakes: Using the full canvas for routine messages where AIM is enough
Filling boxes in isolation without checking they serve the same intent
Forgetting partners, especially a critic who will poke holes before the audience does
steps: Start with AIM: audience (primary and secondary) and intended result
Ask why you are the right messenger and how to cover any credibility gap
List possible channels and choose a mix
Gather assets: stories, data, images, and placeholders for what you still need
Plan activities and partners who will help the message reach and persuade
Structure the message, for example contrasting what is with what could be
Test with a small audience before release
situations: Planning a major company announcement
Preparing a keynote or TED-style talk
Running a fundraising campaign
Winning support for a community proposal

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Part 1, Chapter 1, section 'Beyond AIM: The Leadership Communication Canvas', pp. 14-24
source.underlying_research: Adapted from Osterwalder and Pigneur's Business Model Generation; structure guidance from Nancy Duarte's Resonate (sparkline, Figure 1.4) and Jim Collins on big goals. Practitioner frameworks, not tested empirically.

insights.confidence_rationale: Read directly in the Wiley Chapter 1 excerpt. A credible teaching framework used at Stanford GSB, but untested; Medium for credible expert practice.

insights.name: Verbal, Vocal, Visual: The Delivery Recipe
insights.explanation: The book breaks spoken delivery into three channels to work on separately. Verbal is what you say: deliberate first and last words, strong openings without filler, smooth transitions, and silence for emphasis. Vocal is how it sounds: a clear, projected voice, varied pace and energy, and few filler words. Visual is what people see: eye contact one thought at a time, a stable stance, natural gestures, and purposeful movement. The same chapter covers derailers that erode credibility, such as fillers, uptalk, and commenting on your own slip-ups; reader notes report the advice is to keep going calmly rather than apologize for a stumble.
insights.when_to_use: Preparing any talk or meeting contribution; diagnosing why a presentation felt weak; giving structured feedback to someone else.
insights.worked_example: A nurse manager is preparing a five-minute update for hospital leaders. Verbal: she cuts her opening apology and starts with the key number. Vocal: she marks two sentences to slow down on and practices projecting to the back of the room. Visual: she plants her feet and lands each point on one person. During the update she loses her place, pauses, and carries on without saying 'sorry, I'm all over the place', and nobody notices.
common_mistakes: Working on all three channels at once instead of one at a time
Apologizing for or commenting on mistakes, which draws attention to them
Assuming visual and vocal delivery matter more than content because of misquoted statistics
steps: Record a practice run
Review the words only: opening, closing, transitions, fillers
Review the voice: volume, pace, variety, uptalk
Review the visuals: stance, eye contact, gestures, movement
Pick one fix per channel for the next run
situations: Rehearsing a presentation
Giving feedback on a colleague's talk
Speaking up in a senior meeting
Delivering a toast

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 2 (Speaking with Conviction), section 'Verbal, Vocal, Visual: Your Recipe for Successful Communication', pp. 29-39; managing derailers pp. 40-43 (self-commenting p. 43)
source.underlying_research: The index lists Albert Mehrabian on pp. 29-30. Mehrabian's 1960s studies on inconsistent feelings messages are often misapplied as a general rule that words carry only 7 percent of meaning; I could not see how the book uses them. The book also cites Cara Hale Alter's The Credibility Code (pp. 40-43).

insights.confidence_rationale: Structure confirmed via the table of contents and index, detail from reader notes. Broad expert consensus among speaking coaches, but the possible reliance on Mehrabian is a caution.

insights.name: Pitch Structure: Problem, Solution, Market, Business, then CUE
insights.explanation: For pitching, the book adopts Chris Lipp's four-part structure from The Startup Pitch: the problem, your solution (what is unique, why you, why this, why now), the market, and the business (go-to-market and how you will make money). It then frames the audience journey as CUE: move listeners from distracted to Curious, then to new Understanding, then to Evangelism, where they want to back you and tell others. A crisp, concrete image of the solution, such as Apple's 'a thousand songs in your pocket', helps build the bridge from problem to solution.
insights.when_to_use: Investor and startup pitches, internal funding requests, sales pitches, and proposals for new projects or community initiatives.
insights.worked_example: A team pitching an internal tool to their division head starts with the problem (engineers lose four hours a week to manual test setup), offers the solution and why their team is right to build it now, sizes the market (300 engineers across five groups), and closes with the business case (two months to build, payback in one quarter). They open with a striking stat to spark curiosity, show a 30-second demo for understanding, and end by asking the head to champion it at the next leadership meeting.
common_mistakes: Leading with the solution before the audience feels the problem
Skipping why you and why now
Ending without asking the audience to do anything, so curiosity never becomes evangelism
steps: State the problem in concrete, audience-relevant terms
Present the solution with a one-line image of what it does
Answer why you, why this, why now
Size the market or reach
Explain the business model or resource ask
Plan how each part moves listeners from curiosity to understanding to advocacy
situations: Pitching investors
Asking leadership to fund a project
Proposing a new initiative to a board

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 4, section Pitching, pp. 59-69 (problem, solution, market, business pp. 60-63; building the bridge pp. 63-68; CUE pp. 68-69)
source.underlying_research: Borrowed from Chris Lipp, The Startup Pitch (index p. 60). Practitioner framework; no empirical testing named.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed via the index and reader notes; a credible practitioner framework from startup coaching but not empirically tested.

insights.name: Manage Anxiety: Reframe as Excitement
insights.explanation: The speaking chapter opens with managing anxiety before moving to delivery. Reader notes report the book's advice to take up space with an open posture, to reframe 'I'm nervous' as 'I'm excited', and to treat a talk more like a conversation to lower the pressure. The book draws on Matt Abrahams's Speaking Up Without Freaking Out and discusses Amy Cuddy's power poses alongside Dana Carney, the co-author who later disavowed the original power pose findings. The reappraisal tip has better evidence than the posture tip.
insights.when_to_use: Before presentations, interviews, difficult conversations, or any moment your heart is racing.
insights.worked_example: Waiting to present to a client, a consultant notices her pulse climbing. Instead of telling herself to calm down, she says quietly, 'I'm excited about this', reminds herself she is just having a conversation with four people, and stands with her shoulders open. Before a parent-teacher conference about her son's behavior, she uses the same reframe.
common_mistakes: Trying to force calm, which is harder than relabeling arousal as excitement
Relying on a two-minute pose as if it were a proven hormone hack
Treating a talk as a performance to be judged rather than a conversation
steps: Notice the physical signs of nerves
Say 'I'm excited' rather than 'calm down'
Adopt an open, grounded posture
Frame the talk as a conversation with individuals
Start with a well-rehearsed opening
situations: Before a big presentation
Waiting for a job interview
Before a hard conversation

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 2, section Managing Your Anxiety, pp. 26-29
source.underlying_research: The book cites Abrahams (pp. 26-27), Cuddy's Presence (pp. 27-28) and Carney (p. 28). Related research (my identification): Brooks (2014), 'Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement', Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 143(3), supports the reframe. Power posing (Carney, Cuddy and Yap 2010, Psychological Science) failed to replicate on hormones (Ranehill et al. 2015), and Carney disavowed it in 2016; small effects on felt power remain debated.

insights.confidence_rationale: Section confirmed via the table of contents and index, detail from reader notes. Reappraisal is supported by experimental research; the power pose component is contested.

insights.name: Four-Pass Video Self-Review
insights.explanation: Watching yourself on video is the fastest way to close the gap between how you think you come across and how you actually do. Reader notes report the book's method of four passes: first watch to get the cringing out of the way; then sound only, to judge words, structure, evidence, and vocal variety; then picture only, to judge body language, gestures, eye contact, and slides; then everything on, forcing yourself to note what you like so you can build on strengths. Schramm makes the same point in interviews: even an unobtrusive phone recording of your side of a meeting reveals fillers, uptalk, and rambling.
insights.when_to_use: Rehearsing a high-stakes talk, after a recorded meeting or webinar, or when you want to improve a habit such as filler words.
insights.worked_example: A sales lead records a practice run of a client pitch on her phone. Pass one she winces and moves on. Pass two, audio only, she hears 14 'sort of's and a weak close. Pass three, muted, she sees she rocks side to side. Pass four she notes that her product demo was crisp and energetic. Her next run fixes the close and the rocking and keeps the demo as is.
common_mistakes: Watching once and only noticing flaws
Trying to fix everything at once
Never recording real meetings, only rehearsals
steps: Record a rehearsal or, with permission, a real meeting
Watch once without notes
Listen with the picture off and note verbal and vocal issues
Watch with the sound off and note visual issues
Watch with everything on and list strengths
Choose one or two changes for next time
situations: Practicing a pitch
Improving filler words
Reviewing a recorded webinar

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, video feedback pp. 151-152 (Chapter 8, Tools of the Trade) per index; four-pass method per reader notes; Think Fast, Talk Smart interview with Matt Abrahams (2020)
source.underlying_research: None named. Related research (my identification): video self-modeling and video feedback studies in skills training show benefits, though results vary by setting.

insights.confidence_rationale: Recording and review is confirmed by the index and in Schramm's own interviews and newsletter; the exact four-pass order comes from one reader's notes, so book placement of the method is not fully verified.

research_notes:
VERIFICATION PASS (2026-11-04): Network access opened. I read the Wiley product page, the Wiley excerpt PDFs (full Chapter 1, table of contents, and index), the GBV scanned contents, the Five Books Abrahams interview, the Think Fast, Talk Smart transcript, the Stanford GSB storytelling article, the PlayFull podcast show notes, the Ideas on Stage interview page, the TED Blog Q&A, five Substack posts, and Goodreads reader reviews. O'Reilly (access denied and bot check), Google Books search inside (captcha), Blinkist, Medium, and summary.com were not readable. Because only Chapter 1 could be read in full, chapters 2 to 9 were checked through the table of contents, the index (which gives page-level topic locations), and reader notes; these confirm that topics appear in the book but not the exact wording of the advice.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: JD Schramm with Kara Levy, foreword by Joel Peterson (Wiley credits Peterson as 'Foreword by'; resolves the earlier open question; one Goodreads reviewer calls it a preface). Wiley, January 2020, 240 pages, hardcover 9781119550099, ebook 9781119550167 (another ebook ISBN, 9781119550143, appears at a German retailer). Five Books lists the author as J D Schramm and Abrahams recommends the book, singling out AIM.

STRUCTURE (verified): Foreword; Introduction (Individuality, Relevance, Iteration, Feedback, Stakes). Part 1: Ch1 Adopting a Communication Mindset (Know Your AIM p. 3; Leadership Communication Canvas p. 14); Ch2 Speaking with Conviction (Managing Your Anxiety p. 26; Verbal, Vocal, Visual p. 29); Ch3 Writing for Impact (Active p. 46, Brief p. 47, Clear p. 48, Synthesis > Summary p. 48, Style and Content p. 50, Editing p. 53). Part 2: Ch4 Goal (Pitching p. 59, Storytelling p. 69, Disclosing Personally p. 82); Ch5 Setting (Meetings p. 91, Virtual Meetings p. 97, On Stage p. 99, Co-presenting p. 101, Fielding Questions p. 103, Slides p. 107); Ch6 Identity (Second Language p. 112, LGBTQ p. 113, Women p. 123, Rookie p. 129, Veteran p. 131). Part 3: Ch7 Being Coached p. 141; Ch8 Coaching Others p. 147; Ch9 Coaching Culture p. 157. Epilogue; Appendices A Power Verbs, B Memo on the Quality of Memos, C Glenn Kramon writing tips, D Leadership Communication Bookshelf; Bibliography. The first pass wrongly put all coaching in a single Chapter 7.

LOW-RATED INSIGHTS: 07 story spine is Schramm's own (podcast show notes) but absent from the book index; 12 virtual meetings section confirmed but only topics are known; 13 slowing down and uptalk tied to the book, lower register only to the newsletter; 14 clarity and pace for second-language speakers tied to the book, the Blinkist accent claim not confirmed. All retained at Low per user decision.

UNDERLYING RESEARCH: Book-cited sources are marked as such in each insight. Studies described as 'my identification' are related evidence, not book citations; citations were checked for authors, year, and journal.
